messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 43
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Physical Therapist
  trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
  pcl5: 77

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell, Event Recall: Talking about the event, Trauma-Related Events: Trauma-related events
  Maladaptive Strategies: Compulsive Spending: I spend money impulsively to distract or comfort myself, Stay Near Exit: make sure to stay close to exit, Drug Use: take drugs
  Threat: Noticing Weapons: I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment, Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
  Memory: More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things, No Coherent Story: I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself, Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame
  Negative Appraisals: Thought Avoidance: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it, Unrecognisable Self: The person I have become is unrecognisable to me, Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened

Vignette:
Malia had been a physical therapist for years, and at 43 she had built a life that was steady on the surface: work she was good at, a long-term relationship, and the confidence of someone who was used to helping other people recover. That changed after a work-related accident that she still struggled to describe in a clean sequence, even to herself. In the version she could manage, there had been a routine session that went wrong in a matter of seconds, and a patient ended up seriously injured in a way Malia had not expected and could not stop. What stayed with her was not a neat story but fragments that arrived with the force of the original moment: the abruptness of it, the shock of realizing something had gone very wrong, and the immediate shame that followed. When she tried to speak about it later, she would often stall or change the subject, saying she “couldn’t tell it right,” and then going quiet because putting the event into words made it feel too immediate, too exposing. She described the memory as more vivid and more real than ordinary memories, as if it were preserved in sharper detail than anything else in her life. Certain parts came back without warning, not as a calm recollection but as a sudden re-entry into the scene, with the feeling that she was there again and that the wrongness of it was happening all over.

In the months that followed, Malia began organizing her days around the possibility of being caught off guard by reminders. She noticed that the smell of alcohol was particularly difficult, not because alcohol had been a central feature of the accident, but because it seemed to carry her back to the emotional atmosphere of that period and to the social situations in which she had first had to talk about what happened. If someone at a restaurant opened a drink near her, or if she passed someone carrying alcohol in a hallway or parking lot, her body would tense before she had fully registered why. She also became wary of conversations that might turn toward the event. If a colleague asked a direct question, or if a friend tried to check in by saying they wanted to “hear the whole story,” Malia would feel herself closing down. She was convinced that if she thought too much about what happened she would not be able to handle it, so she tried to keep those thoughts at a distance, even when that meant withdrawing from the very people who wanted to support her. Trauma-related events also unsettled her: hearing about injuries at work, seeing a workplace incident in the news, or encountering any story that carried a similar tone of sudden catastrophe could pull her into the same fixed, distressed state.

Malia’s sense of danger had become unusually broad. In almost any environment, she found herself scanning for potential weapons or dangerous objects, not because she believed she was in immediate peril every moment, but because she no longer trusted ordinary spaces to stay ordinary. A kitchen counter, a tool drawer at work, even the shape of a heavy object left on a chair could catch her attention and keep it there. At times she described feeling abruptly flooded by fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, as though those emotions rose in her before she could sort them out. On harder days, she would also experience moments in which she felt and acted as if the stressful experience were happening again, enough that her partner noticed she had gone pale, stopped speaking, or was staring at something that was not in front of her. These moments were frightening not only because they felt so real, but because they seemed to confirm her fear that she had become someone fundamentally altered by what had happened. She had come to believe that the person she was now was unrecognisable to her, someone less certain, more guarded, and harder to live with than the woman she had been before.

At the center of Malia’s suffering was shame. When the memory surfaced, she felt intense shame, and along with it a punishing certainty that she had not done enough to stop what happened. She told herself she would never forgive herself for that inaction, even while another part of her recognized that in the moment she had been overwhelmed and unable to process the speed of events. That recognition did little to soften the self-condemnation. After work, she often rushed out close to the exit, choosing seats and positions that let her leave quickly if needed. Over time she also began spending money impulsively to distract or comfort herself, buying things she did not need and then regretting it later. At other times she took drugs to blunt the intensity of what she felt, especially after a difficult shift or after an unexpected reminder set off a wave of distress. These habits accumulated quietly and left their own consequences, including strain in her relationship and growing worry about how much of herself was now being organized around avoidance and escape.

By the time she sought help, Malia was exhausted by living as though every day might contain an ambush of memory, shame, or alarm. She did not want to lose her career or her relationship, and she was frightened by how much smaller her life had become. What finally brought her in was the realization that even ordinary moments at work — walking past supply rooms, entering treatment spaces, speaking with colleagues about cases that resembled her own — had become saturated with dread. She wanted to be able to talk about what happened without feeling that she would fall apart, and she was most afraid that if nothing changed she would remain trapped in the version of herself she now found unrecognisable.
